title: A job interview for a developer

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Thanks for coming in. Could you tell me a little about your background?

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.text: Sure. I've been a web developer for about five years. I started in a small agency, and for the last two years I've been working on mobile payment apps.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Interesting. What would you say is your biggest achievement?

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.text: Last year our team won a national data challenge. I was responsible for cleaning the data and building the dashboard.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: And why do you want to leave your current job?

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.text: I enjoy it, but I'd like to work on larger projects and with international teams. I'm also improving my English for that reason.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Great. The position is fully remote, but we have a team meeting every Monday at nine.

title: A short lecture on urban heat

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Today we're looking at a phenomenon called the urban heat island. Simply put, cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: There are three main causes. First, materials like concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Second, there are fewer trees, so there is less shade. Third, cars and air conditioners produce extra heat.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Why does this matter? Higher temperatures increase energy use and can be dangerous for elderly people.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Fortunately, there are solutions. Planting trees, painting roofs white and creating green spaces can reduce temperatures significantly.

questions.prompt: What is an urban heat island?
options: A hot island near a city
A city that is warmer than the countryside around it

questions.prompt: How many main causes does the lecturer mention?
Which is NOT mentioned as a solution?
Concrete releases heat at night.
questions.explanation: "Absorb heat during the day and release it at night."

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: What I'd like us to consider today is not whether African cities will grow, but how. By 2050, Lagos alone may well exceed thirty million inhabitants.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: With respect, isn't the bigger issue that most of that growth will be informal? Planning tends to lag years behind.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: That's a fair point. Rarely do master plans anticipate how quickly settlements appear. Kigali, however, is often cited as a partial exception.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Partly, yes, but critics argue its success came at a social cost, with low-income residents relocated to the edges.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Exactly — which brings me to this week's essay: to what extent can rapid urbanisation be both orderly and fair?
